lessons.title: sprintf
intro: sprintf works like printf, but writes into a char array instead of the screen: sprintf(buf, "%d-%02d-%02d", y, m, d) builds the text "2026-11-04" in buf.
It's how C programs build file names, messages and keys. snprintf(buf, size, …) is the safe version: it never writes more than size characters, even if the result is longer.
The array must be big enough for every character plus the closing '\0'. sprintf can't know how big buf is, which is why snprintf was added later.

exercises.prompt: Where does sprintf write its result?
options: Into the char array you give it

exercises.explanation: %03d pads with zeros to 3 digits, and puts prints the buffer.

exercises.prompt: Why is snprintf safer than sprintf?
options: It never writes more than the size you give it
exercises.explanation: Writing past the end of an array is one of the most common security holes in C.

exercises.prompt: This program writes past the end of buf. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explanation: "123456" needs 7 chars with the '\0'. buf has to be bigger (or use snprintf).

options: The number of characters it wrote

lessons.title: sscanf
intro: sscanf is the opposite: it reads values out of a string, with the same formats as scanf. sscanf("14.11.2026", "%d.%d.%d", &d, &m, &y) splits a date.
It returns how many values it could read. That's the way to check input: if the result isn't the number you expected, the text had the wrong form.
Because the string doesn't change, you can try several formats one after another on the same text. scanf reading from the keyboard can't go back like that.

code: printf("%-12s day %d, month %d, year %d\n", s, d, m, y);
printf("%-12s day %d, month %d, year %d (US)\n", s, d, m, y);

exercises.explanation: The first s stands for string, just like in sprintf.
%d reads 10, %s reads apples: sscanf read 2 values and returns 2.

exercises.prompt: Read two numbers from the string pos.
exercises.explanation: Both values must be read, so the result must be 2.

options: To find out if the text had the expected form
exercises.explanation: "tomorrow" gives 0: no number could be read.

exercises.prompt: sscanf("7 3", "%d %d", &a, &b) sets a and b to:
exercises.explanation: Spaces in the format skip spaces in the text.

exercises.prompt: What's the advantage of fgets + sscanf over scanf alone?
options: You read a whole line first and can try several formats on it
exercises.explanation: If the line is wrong, you skip it and read the next one, instead of getting stuck.

lessons.title: Reading Records
intro: Real data comes in lines: names, numbers, dates. The safe pattern is fgets to read one line, then sscanf to take it apart, and the return value to skip bad lines.
This combination is how Unix tools, config files and log readers have read text for 50 years. It never gets stuck on a bad line the way scanf can.
In the example, each line holds a name and a score. The bad line is reported and skipped.

code: printf("total %d, best %s with %d\n", total, best_name, best);

exercises.prompt: Why read a line with fgets first, then use sscanf?
options: A bad line can be skipped without getting stuck
exercises.explanation: scanf leaves the bad text waiting in the input, and the next scanf fails on it again.
The word is read, but there's no number after it.

exercises.prompt: Skip the line if it doesn't have both values.
exercises.explanation: Anything other than 2 means the line was bad.

exercises.prompt: What does the example print last?
exercises.explanation: 70 + 95 + 80 = 245, and dmr has the highest score.

exercises.prompt: Why strcpy(best_name, name) instead of best_name = name?
options: Arrays can't be assigned; the characters must be copied
exercises.explanation: And name is overwritten by the next line anyway.

exercises.prompt: What does continue do inside the while loop?
options: Jumps to the next round, skipping the rest of the loop body
exercises.explanation: The total isn't changed for the bad line.
